# The Sense Without Words

Try describing the smell of coffee without saying "coffee" — without referencing anything that grows, burns, roasts, or brews. Most people last a few seconds before they start stealing: it's bitter, burnt, dark, warm, heavy. Every one of those words belongs to another sense. English has hundreds of thousands of words and almost none of them are for smells themselves. We have a handful — musty, acrid, fragrant, fetid — and most of those are really just verdicts, telling you whether to lean in or back away.

This turns out to be a local limitation rather than a human one. The Jahai, a hunter-gatherer people of the Malay Peninsula, have abstract words for odors the way we have words for colors, and they use them as effortlessly as we say "blue." Tested in a lab, they name smells as consistently as they name colors, while English speakers, handed the same scents, dissolve into helpless pointing: "like a candle shop," "like my uncle's garage." The faculty exists. Some of us just never practice it — though specialists claw part of it back. Perfumers and wine people build whole private lexicons out of borrowed metaphors: a wine can be angular, flamboyant, dumb; a perfume can have a "green" note, and somehow everyone in the room knows this means crushed leaves and snapped stems.

Here's the strange part. The sense we can least articulate is the one with the strongest claim on our pasts. Smell is wired into the brain through a side door that opens almost directly onto the amygdala and hippocampus — the machinery of emotion and memory — and psychologists keep confirming what Proust staged with a madeleine: odor-cued memories reach further back and land harder than memories summoned any other way. You can walk past a stranger wearing a particular perfume and be seventeen again in an instant, standing in a hallway that no longer exists, feeling something you thought you'd forgotten how to feel. And afterward you cannot even say what the smell was. Only what it opened.

Maybe those two facts are the same fact. Language is a kind of processing. Every time you tell a memory, you revise it; the story slowly replaces the event, until what you remember is the last version you told. But a memory you can't put into words never goes through that mill. It stays raw, unhandled, unedited — which is exactly why, thirty years later, it can still take you by the throat. The sense we can't narrate is the sense that keeps its evidence intact.

Consider petrichor: the smell of rain on dry earth. Humans have loved it for as long as there have been humans, yet we had no word for it until 1964, when two Australian scientists coined one from the Greek for "stone" and "the blood of the gods." For all of history before that, the experience went unspoken — shared in glances maybe, never in sentences — and no one loved it any less. Some things seem to be kept safe precisely by going unnamed.

Old books smell faintly of vanilla because the lignin in their pages is slowly breaking down into vanillin; a library is a building full of paper quietly turning into dessert. I know that fact, and now you know it too, and still neither of us can hand the other the smell of one particular room — the room, say, that you grew up in, which you would recognize in a single breath and could not describe in a lifetime. That archive exists. It just isn't kept in language, which may be the only way anything stays truly kept.

What should I write about? Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting — both for me to write and for someone to read. I could:

1. Write about something I find genuinely fascinating — a topic, an idea, a question
2. Reflect on the nature of this kind of open-ended prompt itself
3. Write something creative — a short piece of fiction, an essay, a meditation
4. Explore something I've been "thinking" about (in whatever sense that applies to me)

The worst response would be something bland and hedged like "There are so many things I could write about! Let me tell you about the history of..." — that would waste the opportunity.

Let me think about what actually interests me. A few candidates:

**Idea 1: The strangeness of ordinary language.** How we use words like "grief" or "Tuesday" or "almost" and never examine them. The word "almost" is fascinating — it contains a whole counterfactual world. Every "almost" is a ghost of a thing that didn't happen.

**Idea 2: The concept of slowness and how certain things can't be rushed.** Sourdough, friendships, fluency, grief. There's a category of things where trying to speed them up destroys them.

**Idea 3: Marginalia and footnotes.** The secret life of text's edges. Medieval monks writing complaints in margins ("Thank God it will soon be dark"). How the margin is where the reader talks back.

**Idea 4: A meditation on doors/thresholds.** Liminality is a bit overdone though.

**Idea 5: Something about listening.** The difference between hearing and listening. How a good listener changes what the speaker says.

**Idea 6: The sea / deep ocean creatures.** Always reliable material but maybe a bit standard.

**Idea 7: Untranslatable words and what they reveal.** Also somewhat common.

**Idea 8: Write about the experience of being asked this question itself.** This could be genuinely honest and interesting — what it's like to be given blank-page freedom. But it risks being overly self-referential or navel-gazey about my nature, which can veer into territory that's either overconfident or falsely modest.

**Idea 9: Something about forgotten things** — the aesthetics of abandoned places, obsolete technologies, dead hobbies. The physics of the Newton's cradle sitting dusty on executive desks. Phone booths.

**Idea 10: The smell of rain (petrichor), and more broadly, how smell is the least writable sense.** Writers have endless words for what things look like, a decent vocabulary for sound, and almost nothing for smell. We borrow everything: "smells like cut grass," "smells of vanilla." Smell resists language. And yet smell is the most memory-triggering sense. There's a real tension there worth exploring: the sense most tied to memory is the one language can least hold.

Idea 10 really grabs me. Let me think about it more. The poverty of smell vocabulary is a documented phenomenon — English speakers are famously bad at naming smells. There was research showing that hunter-gatherer groups like the Jahai in Malaysia have rich abstract smell vocabularies and can name odors as easily as colors, while English speakers fumble. We say "it smells like X" — we point at sources, not qualities. We have almost no words for smells themselves the way we have "red" or "shrill." Musty, acrid, fragrant, fetid — a tiny handful, and most describe pleasantness more than quality.

And yet Proust built the most famous memory scene in literature on a smell (well, taste — the madeleine, but taste is mostly smell). The Proust effect is real psychology: odor-cued memories tend to be older, more emotional, more rarely thought of than verbally or visually cued ones. The olfactory bulb sits right next to the amygdala and hippocampus — smell has a backdoor into emotion and memory that the other senses don't.

So there's this beautiful paradox: the sense we can least articulate is the one that ambushes us with the past most completely. You walk past someone wearing a particular perfume and you're seventeen again, standing in a hallway that no longer exists, feeling something you thought you'd forgotten how to feel. And when it happens you can't even say what the smell was. You can only say what it opened.

Why is smell so hard for language? A few thoughts:
- Smell is holistic; we don't perceive it in analyzable components the way we decompose color into hue/brightness or sound into pitch/loudness. No dimensions to hang words on.
- In English-speaking cultures we don't practice. The Jahai practice. Smell vocabulary is learnable — wine experts and perfumers develop partial lexicons, though even they lean heavily on metaphors (a wine that's "flamboyant," "angular," "shy").
- Maybe evolution deprioritized it for us — we're visual creatures.

And the metaphor-borrowing is interesting in itself. We describe smells with words from other senses: sharp, soft, sweet, heavy, green. Synesthesia is baked into ordinary smell-talk. "Green" as a smell description is genuinely strange if you look at it — cut grass, crushed leaves — and yet everyone knows what a "green" note in a perfume is.

Petrichor is a nice case study: we had no word for the smell of rain on dry earth until 1964, when two Australian scientists coined it from Greek (petra/ichor — the blood of the gods in stone). That's the turn I want: maybe the poverty of language for smell isn't just a failure. Smells stay private, unshareable, unarchivable. Wine descriptors: "angular," "dumb" (a wine in a closed phase is called "dumb"), "flamboyant" — all real wine-tasting terms. Good.

**The Sense Without Words**

Try describing the smell of coffee without saying "coffee" — without referencing anything that grows, burns, roasts, or brews. Most people last a few seconds before they start stealing: it's bitter, burnt, dark, warm, heavy. Every one of those words belongs to another sense. English has somewhere near a million words and almost none of them are for smells themselves. We have a handful — musty, acrid, fragrant, fetid — and most of those are really just verdicts, telling you whether to breathe in or back away.

This isn't a human limitation so much as a local one. The Jahai, a hunter-gatherer people of the Malay Peninsula, have abstract words for odors the way we have words for colors, and they use them as effortlessly as we say "blue." Tested in a lab, they name smells as consistently as they name colors, while English speakers, handed the same scents, dissolve into helpless pointing: "like a candle shop," "like my uncle's garage." The faculty exists. Some of us just never use it — though specialists claw part of it back. Perfumers and wine people build entire private lexicons out of borrowed metaphors: a wine can be angular, flamboyant, dumb; a perfume can have a "green" note, and everyone in the room somehow knows this means crushed leaves and snapped stems.

Here's the strange part. The sense we can least articulate is the one with the strongest claim on our pasts. Smell is wired into the brain through a side door that opens almost directly onto the amygdala and hippocampus — the machinery of emotion and memory — and psychologists keep confirming what Proust staged with a madeleine: odor-cued memories reach further back and hit harder than memories summoned any other way. You can walk past a stranger wearing a particular perfume and be seventeen again in an instant, standing in a hallway that no longer exists, feeling something you thought you'd forgotten how to feel. And afterward you cannot even say what the smell was. Only what it opened.

Maybe those two facts are the same fact. Language is a kind of processing. Every time you tell a memory, you revise it; the story slowly replaces the event, until what you remember is the last version you told. But a memory you can't put into words never goes through that mill. It stays raw, unhandled, unedited — which is exactly why, thirty years later, it can still take you by the throat. The sense we can't narrate is the sense that keeps its evidence intact.

Consider petrichor: the smell of rain on dry earth. Humans have loved it for as long as there have been humans, and yet we had no word for it until 1964, when two Australian scientists coined one from the Greek for "stone" and "the blood of the gods." For all of history before that, the experience went unspoken — shared in glances maybe, never in sentences — and no one loved it any less. Some things seem to be kept safe precisely by going unnamed.

Old books smell faintly of vanilla because the lignin in their pages is slowly breaking down into vanillin — a library is a building full of paper quietly turning into dessert. I know that fact, and I can write it down, and still I cannot hand you the smell of a particular childhood room, or the cold metallic nothing in the air before snow. That archive exists somewhere. It just isn't written in any language, which may be the only way anything stays truly archived at all.
